analysis.one_liner: Bans social media accounts for kids under 13, restricts algorithmic feeds for teens, and conditions school broadband subsidies on blocking social media.
analysis.headline: The Kids Off Social Media Act cleared the Senate Commerce Committee without amendment and was placed on the Senate calendar on June 30, 2025, where it still awaits a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar social media platforms from knowingly letting children under 13 hold accounts, require deletion of existing child accounts and their data, and stop platforms from using personalized recommendation algorithms on anyone under 17. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the rules, and state attorneys general could sue violators. It would also condition schools' discounted federal internet service (the E-Rate program) on blocking social media on school networks and devices, with schools that fail to comply required to repay the subsidies they received.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and their families gain the most: no accounts for kids under 13, deleted child data, no algorithmic recommendation feeds targeting users under 17, and an enforcement path through the FTC and state attorneys general. Schools get a clearer federal framework for keeping social media off subsidized school networks, though at the price of a new certification obligation.

how_it_helps.text: Platforms could no longer knowingly allow children under 13 to hold accounts, and would have to terminate existing child accounts and delete the personal data collected from them.

Platforms could not use personalized recommendation systems — the automated feeds that rank and suggest content — based on the personal data of users under 17, with narrow exceptions for device type, language, and approximate location.

The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the rules as an unfair or deceptive practice, and state attorneys general could sue platforms on behalf of their residents, giving families an enforcement channel beyond federal regulators.

Schools receiving discounted internet service through the federal E-Rate program would have to certify they block social media on school-provided networks and devices, and publish their internet safety policies to the FCC.

analysis.who_pays: Social media platforms bear compliance costs, the loss of young users' engagement, and litigation exposure to state attorneys general. School districts bear the cost of filtering and monitoring technology and risk repaying E-Rate broadband subsidies if they fail to certify and enforce compliance. Teens lose algorithmically curated feeds.
analysis.who_pays_short: Social media platforms and school districts

drawbacks.text: The bill does not require platforms to verify users' ages. It explicitly says a platform is not required to implement age gating or to collect any age data it does not already collect, so enforcement rests on 'knowledge fairly implied' from objective circumstances — meaning a child who signs up with a false birthdate may simply be invisible to the ban.

Schools that cannot show compliance must repay the E-Rate broadband subsidies they received, and schools that cannot certify compliance in their second year become ineligible for discounted internet service entirely, unless they qualify for a waiver. The funding risk falls on school district budgets, which are generally local and tight.
The platform definition carves out video games, direct messaging, email, online shopping, and other services, so several products popular with minors are not covered by the restrictions at all.
The bill does not ban teens from social media; it only restricts algorithmic recommendations. Teens under 17 can still maintain accounts and see content in chronological or search-based formats.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core child-protection provisions are real but modest: they remove accounts and algorithmic feeds for minors while leaving the platforms' basic business intact, and the design choice to prohibit mandatory age verification means the bill depends on platforms admitting what they know, which is the same gap that lets children sign up today. The school provision piggybacks on filtering most schools already do, but ties a significant federal broadband subsidy to certification, so the cost of noncompliance falls on school budgets — a risk that weighs most heavily on districts with little slack. On balance the bill helps kids more than it costs anyone, but it is a weaker version of what its sponsors describe, and its effectiveness turns on FTC and state enforcement that has not yet been tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill got through committee with bipartisan sponsorship and favorable reporting, but it now sits on the Senate calendar waiting for floor time that has not been scheduled.

narrative.text: Senator Brian Schatz introduced the bill on January 28, 2025, joined by a bipartisan group of senators including Ted Cruz, Chris Murphy, and Angus King.
The Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee ordered the bill reported favorably without amendment on February 5, 2025.

The committee formally reported the bill on June 30, 2025, with Senator Cruz reporting it without amendment (Report No. 119-33), and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 108.
No floor vote has been scheduled, and no House action has taken place, as of the latest action history.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nothing has changed for anyone: children are subject to the same platform rules as before, and social media platforms avoid new restrictions as long as the bill stays on the calendar without a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, platforms avoid new limits

for.name: Brian Schatz
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and assembled a bipartisan group of 12 original co-introducers.

for.name: Ted Cruz

for.what_they_did: Co-introduced the bill and formally reported it out of committee without amendment on June 30, 2025.

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat sponsored the bill, its top Republican co-introduced it and reported it from committee, and the 14 cosponsors split 6 Republicans, 7 Democrats, and 1 Independent; no opposition appears in the record.

industries.industry: Social media platforms and ad-driven tech companies
industries.note: The bill forces deletion of child accounts and their data, bars algorithmic recommendation feeds for users under 17, and exposes platforms to FTC enforcement and state attorneys general lawsuits. Platforms make money from engagement and targeted advertising, so cutting their reach to minors cuts a revenue segment.

Schools must certify social media blocking and monitoring on E-Rate-supported networks and devices as a condition of discounted internet service, and face repayment of subsidies if they knowingly fail to comply. Most schools already filter content under the Children's Internet Protection Act, so the added cost is modest, but the funding condition creates real budget risk for districts that miss certification deadlines.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has cleared committee on a favorable report and sits on the Senate calendar, but most bills at this stage never receive floor time unless leadership schedules them or they are attached to a larger package. With bipartisan committee backing it is a plausible candidate for a floor vote or for inclusion in broader tech or kids' safety legislation, but it faces no scheduling guarantee, and the House has not yet acted on a companion.
